138.subtitle: Free of every adjunct, and the circle of teachers

commentary.meaning: Six names by the count most lists follow, and the verse crosses the whole theological spectrum in thirty-two syllables. It opens by stripping her of everything: not one upādhi, not one limiting condition of body or name or circumstance, adheres to her. It closes by identifying her with the most concrete institution the tradition possesses — the succession of teachers, reckoned as a circle, through whom the practice is actually handed on. Between those two poles stand the wife who keeps her vow to Sadāśiva, the mistress of the transmitted doctrine, and two items that are barely names at all: sādhu, the good, and the single vowel ī. The argument of the verse is that the freedom asserted in the first name is not a withdrawal. The one who has no attributes is precisely the one who owns the tradition, sits in the succession, and can be reached through any member of it. What is unconditioned turns out to be met in the most conditioned place there is — a particular teacher, in a particular room.
commentary.history:
Upādhi is the word to take apart first, because everything else in the verse is arranged around it. It is built from upa-ā-√dhā, to place near or set upon: something laid alongside a thing which lends that thing an appearance not its own. The illustration the Vedāntins use is a clear crystal set beside a red hibiscus flower. The crystal looks red. Nothing has happened to the crystal. Remove the flower and the redness goes with it, because the redness was never a property of the stone but of the arrangement. In that vocabulary a body is an upādhi, a name is an upādhi, a caste, an age, a set of circumstances, a role — everything, in short, by which one thing is told apart from another. The other standard image is spatial: the space inside a pot is not a piece of space, and when the pot breaks nothing is released, because nothing was ever confined. Note that the same word does entirely different work in logic, where a Naiyāyika's upādhi is the hidden extra condition that spoils an inference. The tantric and Vedāntic sense is the one operating here.

Vinirmuktā piles two prefixes of removal onto the participle of √muc, to loose. Vi and nis both mean away or out, so the word is emphatic in a way that plain muktā would not be: not merely free but let go of altogether, on every side. And sarva makes the sweep total. It is one of the strongest negations in the hymn, and the hymn immediately follows it by giving her a husband.

That is not carelessness. Sadāśiva, the ever-auspicious, is a technical figure: the fifth of the five whose corpses formed her couch fifty-odd verses earlier, and, in the thirty-six-tattva scheme the Śaiva schools work with, the level at which the undivided begins to distinguish itself into I and this. To call her his pativratā is to use a term with real weight. A vrata is a binding observance undertaken deliberately, and the pativratā is the woman for whom the husband is the observance. The stotra has used marital language before with a constitutional rather than a sentimental edge, and the same word will return nine verses on, when she is called priyavratā, fond of her vow. Placed immediately after sarvopādhivinirmuktā, the name says that a being under no constraint whatever can nevertheless bind herself, and that this is what a vow is.

Sampradāya rewards the same treatment. It is sam-pra-√dā, to hand over completely, and the noun means both the act of handing on and what is handed on. A Sanskrit tradition is therefore literally a gift passed hand to hand, and its two nearest synonyms carry the same freight: āgama is that which has come down, paramparā is one-after-another. In Indian intellectual life this is not decoration. A doctrine with no sampradāya has no standing, and the compliment paid to a scholar is that he is sampradāyavit, one who knows how the thing has been transmitted. To call her the mistress of the sampradāya is to say that the authority of the chain does not come from the chain.

Then the counting problem. As recited, the second line reads sādhvī — chaste, virtuous, a good woman — and one name is what the ear hears. The enumerations that must arrive at exactly one thousand generally split it into two, sādhu and ī, glossing the first as goodness and the second as the bare vowel, which the lexicons do record as a name of Lakṣmī. Lists differ, and this is one of several places in the thousand where the total is maintained by a decision of this kind. It is worth knowing about rather than being troubled by: a text recited as continuous verse and a text enumerated as a list of a thousand items are two different objects, and they do not always divide in the same places.

The last name is the practical one. Guru is an ordinary adjective meaning heavy — the grammarians use it of a long syllable — and the teacher is the one with weight. A popular etymology found in the later handbooks reads the two syllables separately, gu as darkness and ru as its removal; it is not a historical derivation but it tells you what the tradition thinks the word is for. What matters here is the plural. Maṇḍala is a circle, a ring, an assembled company. Śrīvidyā ritual worships the teachers as a body before it worships anything else, arranged in three streams: the divine, the perfected and the human, with the practitioner's own line at the near end of the third. To be embodied as that circle is to be reachable through any point on it.
commentary.practice:
Four of the six names begin with s, and the first line is nothing but sibilants and dentals: sarvopādhivinirmuktā sadāśivapativratā. Both quarters are eight syllables, both end in the long ā of the feminine nominative, and reciters who are going quickly tend to let the two run together into one sixteen-syllable smear. Set them apart by their opening vowels — sar with a short a, sa-dā with a short a and then a long one — and the line divides itself.

The first name hides the commonest vowel fusion in the hymn after e. Sarva ends in a short a, upādhi begins with a short u, and a followed by u gives o. So the o of sarvopādhi is a seam, exactly as the e of maheśvara is, and the word means all the adjuncts rather than anything to do with sarva-o. The second line has the e version of the same rule: sampradāya plus īśvarī, a plus ī, giving sampradāyeśvarī.

The clusters worth isolating are four. Mpr in sampradāya is three consonants — labial nasal, labial stop, then r — and English will want to insert a vowel; keep the lips closed through the m and open them once. Dhv in sādhvī is an aspirated dental followed by the v, which in Sanskrit is nearer an English w than a v. Vr in pativratā is the same v with a tapped r after it. And ṇḍ in maṇḍala is the retroflex pair, tongue-tip curled back for both, immediately followed by a dental l — the sharpest back-to-front movement in the verse, and the same shape as in candramaṇḍala earlier in the hymn.

There are exactly three retroflex sounds in the whole verse and they are all in the last name: the ṇ and ḍ of maṇḍala and the ṇ of rūpiṇī. Everything before that is dental or labial. Say the first line with the tongue-tip forward and let the last word be the only place it moves back, and the verse acquires a shape.

When the verse is used as archanā, with each name in the dative followed by namaḥ, this is one of the most instructive places in the whole nāmāvalī. The ā-stems take -āyai: sarvopādhivinirmuktāyai, sadāśivapativratāyai. The ī-stems take -yai with the ī turning into a glide: sampradāyeśvaryai, gurumaṇḍalarūpiṇyai. And then, if you are following the enumeration that splits the fourth name, you say sādhune — a masculine and neuter dative, the ending of a u-stem, dropped without warning into a sequence of feminine forms — followed by the single syllable yai for the vowel ī. Nothing else in the thousand sounds like that. Reciters who have never noticed the split hear it at once here, because the mouth has to do something it has not done for hundreds of names.

One long-vowel warning. Sadāśiva has a long ā in its second syllable and short vowels everywhere else, and it is easy to lengthen the i of śiva by analogy with the many names in this hymn that end in -īśa. It does not have one. Sadā means always; śiva is short, twice.

As for what the verse asks of the person saying it: the movement is from a being with no conditions to a company of human beings with names and dates. If the first name is taken as the whole content, the last one becomes sentimental, a gesture toward one's teachers. Taken in sequence they say something harder — that the unconditioned has no other address.

139.subtitle: Beyond the kula, and made of honey

commentary.meaning: Nine names, and the verse is held together by sound before it is held together by argument. The first line runs k, then bh, then three names beginning with m; the second line runs g, g, k, g. Inside that pattern the hymn does something it seldom risks: it puts a technical term of Kaula doctrine at the head of the line, says she has risen clean out of the kula, and then follows it with three of the oldest and plainest words in the language — māyā, madhumatī, mahī. Illusion, honey, earth. Two of those are Vedic and one is the great problem-word of later philosophy, and all three are handed to her without comment. The second line then assembles a retinue that no one would have predicted: the disorderly troops who follow Śiva, and the hidden ones who sit on buried treasure. It ends where the previous verse ended, on the teacher. Guru is the last word of both, which is not accidental. This is the middle panel of a three-verse sequence about transmission.
commentary.history:
Kula means a herd, a family, a house, a lineage. The tantric schools took the ordinary word and made it carry a great deal: the body, the assembly of practitioners, the whole field of what is manifest and female and embodied, set against akula, the unmanifest ground identified with Śiva. The Kaula traditions take their name from it, and Śrīvidyā inherits both the vocabulary and a long internal argument about how far the older Kaula practices should be followed literally. Kulottīrṇa is a term of art in that argument. Uttīrṇa is the past participle of ud-√tṝ, to cross up and out — the word used of coming up out of a river onto the bank. What has crossed out of the kula is past the distinctions the kula is built on. Commentators gloss the name in several ways and do not agree: kula as the body, so that she is not embodied; kula as the triad of knower, known and knowing, so that she is past the structure of experience itself; kula as the Kaula order, so that she stands above the very school that specialises in her. The tradition is comfortable with the third reading, which is a piece of self-limitation worth noticing in a text that is otherwise happy to advertise.

Bhaga is one of the richest words in the verse. Its root sense is a share or portion, from √bhaj, to divide and to allot, and it gives bhāgya, one's allotted fortune, and bhagavat, the one who possesses the portions. In the Ṛgveda Bhaga is a god, one of the Ādityas, the apportioner who distributes what each is to get. The purāṇic definition, quoted whenever the word bhagavat needs justifying, counts six of these portions: sovereignty, righteousness, fame, beauty, knowledge and detachment. Bhaga is also, in ordinary Sanskrit and in the Kaula ritual vocabulary, the female generative organ, and the school has a goddess Bhagamālinī, garlanded with bhagas, who is one of the fifteen Nityās and presides over one of the enclosures of the Śrīcakra. The commentators divide here, and it is not useful to pretend otherwise: some take bhagārādhyā as worship offered by way of the six excellences, some by way of the bhaga rites of the left-hand path. The name will bear both, and its position in a verse that begins by saying she is above the kula is probably not innocent.

Māyā comes from √mā, to measure, and its Vedic sense is the uncanny craft by which a god produces a form — closer to artistry than to deceit. The pejorative reading arrives later, with the Vedāntic use of the word for the power that makes a single reality appear as many. This school keeps both and adds a third: hrīṃ, the seed-syllable at the heart of her mantra, is called the māyā-bīja, so that saying māyā names a sound as well as a metaphysical function. What the stotra will not do is let the word stay negative. Three names later she is Mahī, the ground everything stands on.

Madhumatī is honey with the possessive suffix -mat: she in whom there is honey. Two traditions stand behind it. The first is the Madhu-vidyā of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, where each thing in the world is declared to be the honey of all beings and all beings the honey of it, a doctrine of reciprocal sweetness that ends by identifying the honey with the self. The second is the yogic use: the literature on absorption gives the name madhumatī to a stage of concentration, associated with the truth-bearing insight of the Yoga Sūtra, and Vyāsa's commentary speaks of the madhubhūmika, the yogin who has reached the honey ground. Mahī, immediately after, is the wide one — an old Vedic name for the earth, and one of the three goddesses invoked side by side in the Āprī hymns along with Iḷā and Sarasvatī. Placing it after māyā is a small argument: what appears is not thereby unreal, and the world she projects is also the floor she is.

The second line changes company. The gaṇas are Śiva's troops, an ill-assorted crowd of attendants under Gaṇeśa's captaincy, and ambā is the nursery word for mother that also stands behind Ambikā. To be their mother is to be responsible for a rabble rather than a court. The Guhyakas take their name from guhya, hidden, from √guh, to cover: they belong to Kubera's household in the northern mountains and keep the buried hoards, and they shade into the yakṣas of the same court, one of whom Kālidāsa exiled and made into the most famous lover in Sanskrit poetry. The name is thus about concealed wealth and, by a pun the tradition enjoys, about secret worship. Then komalāṅgī, soft-limbed, drops the whole apparatus and describes a body. Then gurupriyā, which is grammatically ambiguous in the way the hymn likes: she to whom the teacher is dear, and she who is dear to the teacher, are the same words.
commentary.practice:
Count the syllables before anything else and the verse stops looking crowded. First line: kulottīrṇā four, bhagārādhyā four, māyā two, madhumatī four, mahī two. Second line: gaṇāmbā three, guhyakārādhyā five, komalāṅgī four, gurupriyā four. Nine names in thirty-two syllables is dense even for this hymn, and the two-syllable names in the middle of the first line are where reciters lose their footing, because the ear expects four.

Kulottīrṇā is built on a vowel fusion and on a sandhi rule that governs a great deal of Sanskrit. Kula ends in a short a, uttīrṇa begins with a short u, and a plus u gives o — the same rule you have just met in sarvopādhi. Then the ending: -rṇā, not -rnā. Sanskrit turns a dental n into the retroflex ṇ when an r has preceded it in the same word, which is why the participle is uttīrṇa and not uttīrna. Once you know the rule you will stop being surprised by karṇa, varṇa, pūrṇa and a hundred others.

The two ārādhyā names are the pillars of the verse, one at the end of the first quarter and one in the middle of the second line. Both are joins of a short a with a long ā, giving a single long ā, and both end in the cluster dhy: an aspirated dental with the palatal glide immediately after, released as one gesture and not as d-h-y. Say bhagārādhyā and guhyakārādhyā one after the other as a drill.

Guhyaka also gives the cluster hy. The Sanskrit h is voiced, closer to the h in behind than to the h in house, and the y follows it without a vowel. Do not let it become gu-hi-ya.

The three m-names in the first line are a lesson in vowel quantity and nothing else. Māyā is long and long. Madhumatī is short, short, short, long. Mahī is short, long. Say them in sequence at half speed listening only for length, and the anuṣṭubh will hold itself up. The dh of madhumatī is a genuine aspirate — breath after the stop, not before it — and the h of mahī is a full consonant, not a glide.

In the second line, gaṇāmbā has the retroflex ṇ followed four syllables later by the labial cluster mb, and komalāṅgī has ṅg, where the nasal is guttural, made at the same place as the g it precedes. The tongue does not move between them. That is the same relationship as ñc in pañca, and hearing the two as one family is more useful than memorising the nasal series as a chart.

The datives, if you are using the verse as archanā, include one that catches people out. Kulottīrṇāyai, bhagārādhyāyai, māyāyai, gaṇāmbāyai, guhyakārādhyāyai and gurupriyāyai are all straightforward ā-stems. Madhumatī gives madhumatyai and komalāṅgī gives komalāṅgyai, both with the ī turning into a glide. Mahī gives mahyai, which is only two syllables and sounds so unlike the name it comes from that reciters often reach for something longer.

What to hold while chanting it: the verse begins by putting her outside the system and ends by putting her inside a personal relationship. Nothing between those two points is offered as a reconciliation, and the reciter is not asked to supply one.

140.subtitle: The silent teacher who faces south

commentary.meaning: Five names, and this is the verse that finishes the three-verse block on transmission by saying who the teacher actually is. It begins with the strongest word for freedom the language has: svatantrā, running on her own authority, taking her rule from nothing outside herself. It then makes every system of practice hers, not merely her own school's. And then, having established that she is subject to no tantra, it says she is Dakṣiṇāmūrti — the form of Śiva that sits facing south beneath a banyan and teaches by not speaking. The last two names supply the scene with an audience and a result: the four sages who are permanently boys, and the knowledge of Śiva, which is what the silence conveys and which is described as a gift rather than an achievement. There is a joke in the order, and it is the point of the verse. The goddess who owns all the books is depicted in the one form in the tradition that never opens its mouth.
commentary.history:
Svatantra is not, in origin, a mystical word. It is sva, one's own, plus tantra in its plain sense of framework or governing arrangement, and Sanskrit legal and grammatical texts use it for a person or a term that stands on its own account rather than depending on another. The Kashmirian Śaiva philosophers built their entire system on the abstract noun made from it. Svātantrya, in Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta, is the freedom of consciousness to appear as anything at all — to take the shape of a world, of a limited subject, of a stone — without ever ceasing to be consciousness. It is not freedom from constraint but freedom as a positive capacity, and it is what distinguishes a living awareness from a mirror. When this hymn calls her svatantrā it is using a word that had been given that much weight, and it is worth remembering that fifty verses earlier the hymn made the tantra hers; here the adjective has migrated from the system to the person.

Sarvatantreśī extends the claim past the boundary of the school. There is a real question underneath it. The tantric world was not one thing: Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta and Buddhist tantras coexisted, argued, borrowed and denounced each other, and the standard way of managing this was to arrange the rival revelations in a hierarchy with one's own at the top. This name does something more economical. It does not rank the tantras; it says that all of them are under one authority, which is a way of claiming universality without having to adjudicate.

Then the verse gives her a male form, and not a minor one. Dakṣiṇāmūrti is Śiva as teacher, and in South India he is impossible to avoid: the niche on the south wall of the central shrine of a Śiva temple is his by convention, so that anyone who has walked clockwise round a Cōḻa sanctum has passed him. The iconography is fixed in outline. He is young. He sits under a banyan on a rock, one leg folded, the other foot pressed on the back of a dwarf usually identified as Apasmāra, forgetfulness. One hand is raised in the cinmudrā, the thumb and forefinger joined into a circle with the other three fingers extended, a gesture the commentators read as the joining of the individual and the absolute with the three strands of nature left outside. The remaining hands hold some combination of a rosary, a manuscript, a serpent and a flame. Around him, at his feet, sit sages who are visibly old.

The word dakṣiṇā admits more than one reading and the tradition uses several. The obvious sense is facing south, and the south is Yama's quarter, the direction of death, so that the teacher is turned toward the thing everyone else has arranged not to look at. Dakṣiṇa also means right-handed, skilful and favourable. And dakṣiṇā is the fee given to a teacher or a priest, which lets some commentators read the compound as the form that is itself the offering. There is a further reading, current among those who need to explain why a form of Śiva is being counted among a thousand names of the goddess: dakṣiṇā is a feminine word, and the mūrti can be taken as hers. What the name asserts, on any reading, is that the teaching function is not divided by gender.

Sanaka and the rest are the mind-born sons of Brahmā: Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana and Sanatkumāra. The story is that Brahmā produced them to populate the world and they declined, choosing celibacy and knowledge instead, and that they were fixed by that choice at the age of about five, so that they remain boys for the whole of cosmic time. This produces the paradox the tradition never tires of. Under the banyan the pupils are ancient and the teacher is young; and the pupils, in their own right, are old enough to have been present at the beginning. One of them, Sanatkumāra, is the teacher in the last book of the Chāndogya, where he takes Nārada through the whole ladder of knowledge from grammar to the infinite — so the audience of this silence includes a formidable lecturer.

Śivajñāna is a technical term rather than a description. In the Śaiva schools it names the knowledge that liberates, and the foundational treatise of Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta is called the Śivajñānabodham, the awakening to the knowledge of Śiva. The genitive can be read two ways — knowledge of Śiva and the knowledge that Śiva is — and the tradition means both. What the name adds is pradāyinī: she gives it. The whole three-verse block has been about a chain of teachers and an institution, and it ends by saying that what the institution exists to convey cannot be got by working through the institution. It has to be handed over.
commentary.practice:
The first line divides three, five, eight: svatantrā, sarvatantreśī, dakṣiṇāmūrtirūpiṇī. The caesura therefore falls after the second name, not in the middle of the third, which is a mercy. The second line is two eight-syllable names, evenly split.

The first two names are a deliberate near-repetition and they are the trap. Both contain the cluster ntr — dental n, dental t, and r, three separate articulations with no vowel anywhere among them — and both put it in the same place. Do not let the t vanish. Say sva-tan-trā and sar-va-tan-tre-śī with the n fully closed at the teeth, the t released, and the r as its own tap. This is the same cluster as in mahātantrā and mahāmantrā earlier in the hymn, and it is worth drilling here because the two names come back to back and the difference between them is carried entirely by what surrounds the cluster.

Sarvatantreśī is a fusion: sarvatantra plus īśī, a plus ī giving e. The initial cluster sv in svatantrā is a dental s straight into a v that in Sanskrit is nearer to w than to the English v; there is no vowel between them.

Dakṣiṇāmūrtirūpiṇī is the hardest word in the verse and it is worth taking in pieces. Kṣ is a single conjunct of k and the retroflex ṣ, never the sound of an English x. The ṇ that follows is retroflex too. Then rt, an r followed by a dental t. Then a long ū, and the ending -piṇī with another retroflex ṇ. Three retroflex consonants and a conjunct in eight syllables, and the tongue-tip goes back, forward, back again.

That sets up the single most useful contrast in the verse. The first line ends in -rūpiṇī with a retroflex ṇ; the second line ends in -pradāyinī with a plain dental n. They rhyme to an English ear and they are different sounds. Say the two line-endings one after the other, listening for the tongue-tip: back for rūpiṇī, forward for pradāyinī. If you can hear the difference reliably you have solved most of the retroflex problem in this hymn, because the -inī and -iṇī endings occur in the hundreds.

Sanakādisamārādhyā is three joins, all of them a plus ā giving ā: sanaka and ādi, then sam-ā-rādhyā with its prefix. The word has no conjunct at all until the final dhy, which makes it the one place in the verse where the mouth can rest.

Jñ, in śivajñāna, is pronounced very differently across India — gy in the north, dny in Maharashtra, ny in much of the south — and none of these is wrong in its own region. The value the grammarians describe is a palatal j followed by the palatal nasal ñ, both made with the tongue-body flat against the hard palate.

In archanā: svatantrāyai, sarvatantreśyai, dakṣiṇāmūrtirūpiṇyai, sanakādisamārādhyāyai, śivajñānapradāyinyai. The last two are among the longest datives in the nāmāvalī, and saying them at the ordinary pace of archanā without slurring the -ṇyai and -nyai endings is a good test of whether the retroflex distinction has actually been learned or merely understood.

What to hold while chanting it: the verse describes a teaching situation in which nothing is said, delivered by a hymn that consists of nothing but words. Reciters who find that contradictory are hearing it correctly.

crossReferences.translation: To him who sees the universe as a city seen in a mirror — inside himself, though by his own power of illusion it appears to have arisen outside, as things do in sleep; who at the moment of waking realises nothing but his own self, without a second: to him, in the form of the teacher, to Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, this homage.
crossReferences.relevance: The most famous poem on the figure named in the third name of this verse, and the reason that figure is a teacher at all. The image is precise: a city in a mirror is not a small city, it is no city, and the mirror is not altered by it. Every verse of the stotra ends with the same refrain, which places the guru-form and Dakṣiṇāmūrti in apposition — exactly the identification the previous two verses of the sahasranāma have been building toward.

Note that maunaṃ vyākhyānam is a flat contradiction in Sanskrit as much as in English: vyākhyāna is specifically a spoken commentary, the thing a teacher does out loud.

141.subtitle: A digit of consciousness, and a hymn that names itself

commentary.meaning: Seven names, and one of them describes the act you are performing while you say it. The verse opens in the finest register it has — a single digit of awareness, a bud of bliss that has not yet opened — and then names her love and her kindness in the plainest words available, prema and priya. Then comes the name that turns the hymn around to look at its own reciter: pleased by the reading-through of the names. It is the only self-reference the thousand permits itself outside the framing narrative, and it is placed in the middle of a verse about affection rather than among the reward-verses at the end, which changes its force considerably. After that the verse goes back out into the tradition: a recension of her formula that carries Nandin's name, and the mistress of dancers, which happens to be Nandin's other province. What holds the seven together is the claim that the fine sliver of consciousness at the head of the line takes pleasure in being spoken to.
commentary.history:
Cit is the barest word for awareness the language has — not thought, not mind, not knowledge of anything, simply the fact of there being awareness at all. The hymn has reached for it twice before at moments when it wanted to say what she is rather than what she is like: at the fourth name, where she rises out of a fire-pit made of cit, and again where she is called cinmayī, made of it. Kalā, met earlier in this hymn as the arts and as the digits of the moon, has as its root sense a small division of something larger. Putting the two together produces a deliberate strain. Consciousness is exactly the sort of thing that cannot have parts; a sixteenth of it is not a smaller quantity of it. What the compound points at is the finest thing that is still awareness and not an object of awareness — and the moon is the right image, because a crescent is not a piece of the moon broken off but the whole of it seen at an angle.

Ānandakalikā keeps the sound and changes the figure. A kalikā is a bud, an unopened flower, and it is a near-homonym of kalā without being related to it. A bud is not an incomplete flower; it is a complete thing that has not happened yet. Set beside citkalā the pair says that what she is at her most inward is both very small and entirely unspent.

Preman, from √prī, to please or gladden, is the ordinary Sanskrit word for affection, used of parents and friends as readily as of lovers. The devotional theorists made it technical, distinguishing it from kāma by its direction: kāma wants something for the one who has it, preman for the one it is directed at. Nārada's aphorisms on devotion define bhakti itself as being of the nature of supreme preman. To make it her rūpa, her form, is to say that this is not a disposition she has but the material she consists of. Priyaṅkarī, which follows, is the practical version of the same thing — she who does what is pleasing — and the word carries a nice piece of sandhi, since priyam plus karī becomes priyaṅkarī, the final nasal taking the guttural form of the k it runs into.

The fifth name is the interesting one. Pārāyaṇa is pāra, the far shore, plus ayana, a going: a going to the other side. It is the standard Sanskrit word for reading a text right through from beginning to end, and the metaphor buried in it is a crossing of water. A Rāmāyaṇa pārāyaṇa or a week-long recitation of the Bhāgavata is the same word in use. Nāmapārāyaṇaprītā therefore does not say that she likes being praised. It says that the complete recitation of the thousand names, performed as a passage from one bank to the other, is a sufficient offering — and it says so inside the recitation itself, at name seven hundred and thirty-two, when the reciter is roughly three-quarters of the way across. The tradition surrounds the stotra with elaborate ritual apparatus, and this name quietly asserts that the reading alone will do.

Nandividyā returns to the transmission that occupied the three preceding verses. Nandin, or Nandikeśvara, is Śiva's foremost attendant and gatekeeper, the one whose leave is needed before anyone reaches Śiva at all. A vidyā, in this vocabulary, is specifically a goddess's mantra. The lists of teachers through whom her vidyā descends differ from handbook to handbook, and not all of them include Nandin; the commentators are not agreed about whether the Nandi-vidyā is one of the standard recensions of the fifteen-syllabled formula or a distinct mantra transmitted through him. The general sense is secure even where the detail is not: a form of her mantra bears his name.

Naṭeśvarī closes the verse and ties it back to Nandin by a route that is easy to miss. Naṭa, from the root that gives nṛtya, is a dancer or an actor, and Naṭeśvara is the lord of the dance, the figure the bronzes call Naṭarāja. She is his feminine counterpart, and also, in her own right, the presiding authority over performers. Nandin's connection with the performing arts is old: the manual of dance-gesture called the Abhinayadarpaṇa is attributed to a Nandikeśvara, and the tradition puts Nandin close to Śiva whenever the dance is being performed. This is the third position on dancing the hymn has taken within a hundred verses. Earlier she watched the tāṇḍava; in the next verse she will be said to love the lāsya; here she runs the company.
commentary.practice:
The metre is unusually tidy and will carry you if you notice it: eight, four, four in the first line, and eight, four, four again in the second. Citkalānandakalikā, premarūpā, priyaṅkarī; nāmapārāyaṇaprītā, nandividyā, naṭeśvarī. The two lines answer each other exactly, and each begins with its longest name.

The printed text marks the first join with two avagraha signs, which is a device some editions use to flag a swallowed long vowel. Nothing is pronounced there. Citkalā ends in a long ā, ānandakalikā begins with a long ā, and a long ā plus a long ā gives one long ā, held for the ordinary two beats and no more. The temptation is to make it three beats because the page has two marks on it.

The first word also completes a small collection the reciter has been assembling. The element cit ends in a dental t, and Sanskrit does three different things with it depending on what follows. Before a vowel it voices to d, giving cidagnikuṇḍa in the fourth name of the hymn. Before a nasal it becomes the matching nasal, giving cinmayī. Before an unvoiced stop it simply stays, giving citkalā. One consonant, three outcomes, all three now in the mouth.

Priyaṅkarī is the other sandhi worth pausing over, and it is audible. The name is priyam plus karī, and the final m, standing before a guttural k, is produced as the guttural nasal ṅ — the sound at the end of the English sing, made at the back with the tongue-body against the soft palate. Do not say priyam-karī with the lips closed; the lips never close.

Retroflex discipline is what the second line asks for. Pārāyaṇa has a retroflex ṇ, because the r earlier in the word has triggered the same rule that gave kulottīrṇā its ending in the verse before last. Naṭeśvarī has a retroflex ṭ, and it is the single most-mispronounced consonant in this name; the dental t of madhumatī two verses back is a good thing to say immediately before it as a contrast. Nandividyā, sitting between them, has nothing retroflex at all: two dental n sounds and the conjunct dy, dental d into the palatal glide, which is the same cluster as in vidyā wherever it appears.

Vowel lengths in nāmapārāyaṇaprītā need attention because four of the eight syllables are long and they are not evenly spaced: nā-ma-pā-rā-ya-ṇa-prī-tā. Long, short, long, long, short, short, long, long. Get that wrong and the quarter will not scan.

In archanā the datives run citkalāyai, ānandakalikāyai, premarūpāyai, priyaṅkaryai, nāmapārāyaṇaprītāyai, nandividyāyai, naṭeśvaryai. Note that the fourth and the last are ī-stems taking -yai while the rest take -āyai, and that saying priyaṅkaryai preserves the guttural nasal even though the word has changed shape.

What to hold while chanting: this is the verse in which the text notices you. If the thousand names are being read straight through, the fifth name arrives as a statement about what is happening at that moment in the room, and it is worth letting it land rather than passing over it at the speed of the surrounding epithets. The claim being made is a modest one and therefore easy to underrate — that the reading itself, without any further apparatus, is enough.

crossReferences.translation: It is, toward him, of the nature of the highest love. And it is of the nature of the deathless.
crossReferences.relevance: The definition of devotion in the tradition's most compressed handbook, and the exact phrase behind premarūpā. Two things are worth noticing. Nārada does not say that devotion produces love or expresses love; he says it is of love's form, which is the same construction the sahasranāma uses. And the very next aphorism identifies that form with the deathless, which is why the hymn can put a name about affection immediately after two names about consciousness and bliss without any change of register.

crossReferences.translation: Always proclaiming me, striving, firm in their vows, doing homage to me with devotion, constantly disciplined, they worship.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest respectable statement that saying the names aloud is itself the practice and not a preliminary to it. Kīrtayantaḥ is a present participle — the proclaiming is continuous — and the verse puts it first among the four activities it lists. Nāmapārāyaṇaprītā makes the same claim from the other side, by describing the effect on the one being named.

references.title: Nārada Bhakti Sūtras

references.note: Eighty-four aphorisms, most of them a line long, on what devotion is and how it differs from what resembles it. The first dozen are the relevant ones here. The translation is plain and the notes are restrained, which is what you want for a text whose whole method is definition by exclusion.

Reading even a few pages of it explains why naṭeśvarī is a serious title rather than a poetic one: dance in this tradition is a codified language, and somebody has to be its authority.

Useful for this verse in particular, because it lets you hear how the reciter handles the eight-four-four division of both lines.
